newsitem.title: GREECE: New Greek econ team gets reserved market welcome.
newsitem.headline: New Greek econ team gets reserved market welcome.

text.p: Yannos Papandoniou, Greece's new national economy and finance minister, will bring about continuity in economic policy and harmonise relations with the central bank but raises concerns over fiscal policy, traders said on Wednesday.

"It is a positive development safeguarding policy continuity. The market is now looking for tangible evidence of the new economic team's intentions in the 1997 budget," said Harris Makkas, deputy manager and country treasurer at the Bank of America's Athens branch.
The Greek bourse climbed 0.82 percent to 970.77 points on the news on high turnover of 11 billion drachmas ($46 million).
Other bankers called the changes in the economics team positive but expressed reservations over the concentration of power in one man's hands.
"The first impression is positive but there are some reservations over the concentration of power in one minister's hands," said Spyros Kordopatis, treasurer at Credit Lyonnais.

Other bankers said they now expected a closer working relationship between the central bank and the finance ministry over interest rate policy, an area of friction between the fiscal and the monetary authorities in the past.

Pressed by the need to cut interest costs and slash the budget deficit, the finance ministry had adopted a policy of deep, fast nominal rate cuts on domestic debt paper, compressing real drachma rates. It also resorted to cheap foreign currency borrowing.

On the other hand, the central bank has advocated a more conservative interest rate policy aiming to control the rate of growth of M3 within a preset target zone and keep the drachma broadly stable against the ecu in 1996.

M3 slowed down to 8.3 percent year-on-year in July from 9.9 percent in June, falling within the 6.0-9.0 percent target range for the first time this year. The drachma has appreciated by about 0.68 percent year-to-date against the ecu.
The finance ministry has steered more towards domestic borrowing so far this year at the expense of foreign borrowing. This has drained part of the excess liquidity and helped slow down money growth.

But faced with reported revenue shortfalls and higher than projected rates on state securities, the market worries that the finance ministry will be tempted to finance part of this year's deficit from its forex cash reserves and additional borrowing in foreign currencies.

The departure of hard-working Alexandros Papadopoulos at his own will from the finance ministry has heightened concern on how tough his successor will be in tackling Greece's budget deficit and huge public debt.
Yannos Papandoniou, nicknamed by Papadopoulos "the optimist", has repeatedly emphasised the need for a strict implementation of Greece's European Union convergence plan.

The comparison of actual and estimated figures with those of the EU plan show that Greece has put on a mixed performance over the 1994-1996 period. GDP growth has been the biggest success but inflation the biggest disappointment despite its drop.

"I am really concerned about the fiscal side," said a senior banker. "Papadopoulos was a realist who would go against the tide and decline to sign bills containing spending provisions. Papandoniou's track record does not show that."

He pointed out that Papandoniou was the first minister to succumb to union pressure and sign the productivity bonuses given to civil servants this year which threaten to derail the 1996 budget by an augmented wage bill.
But other bankers said the budget would benefit from public sector savings resulting from restructuring that Papadopoulos is likely to undertake as the new powerful interior minister.
"The budget will be among the primary beneficiaries from the reorganisation of the public sector that I am sure Papadopoulos will undertake," said Kordopatis.
